claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by their ability to form and maintain an ultra-nanocrystalline or dynamically refined near-surface layer during sliding.
The refined near-surface layer reduces friction and wear.
The refined near-surface layer reduces friction and wear by limiting stress localization at the contact interface.
Conventionally processed CoCrFeMnNi or AlCoCrFeNi coatings can have relatively coarse or mixed grain structures.
Refining the initial coating grain size makes it predisposed to form a protective surface layer during sliding.
The proposed comparison uses otherwise controlled coatings with nanocrystalline versus conventional coarse or mixed initial grain structures.
An ultra-nanocrystalline or dynamically refined surface layer evolves during wear.
Sliding-induced shear can trigger near-surface grain refinement and possible amorphization.
The adaptive nanocrystalline layer distributes contact stress.
The adaptive nanocrystalline layer locally increases hardness.
The adaptive layer suppresses adhesive and abrasive wear by lowering interfacial friction.
Initially nanocrystalline coatings will have lower friction coefficients and wear rates than initially coarse coatings.
The initially nanocrystalline coatings will perform better because the protective layer forms more rapidly and remains more stable.
In the coarse-grained baseline, the ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer forms as a wear-induced transformation.
The proposed mechanism should hold for compositionally complex HEA coatings such as CoCrFeMnNi and AlCoCrFeNi when oxidation is minimal.
Reactive oxide formation may dominate wear behavior in highly oxidative or extremely high-temperature environments.
The critical initial grain-size threshold and exact compositional requirements for sustaining the adaptive layer are not quantitatively established.

The hypothesis can be tested by subjecting coarse and engineered nanocrystalline coatings to identical dry sliding tests and measuring wear rate, friction, post-wear microstructure, and near-surface hardness.

Failure of the pre-refined coatings to show a statistically significant friction and wear reduction, or development of similar protective layers regardless of initial grain size, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
